title: Weekly Fixes & Polish (Aug 18-24)
summary: 19 bug fixes and style improvements across calendar, live scoring, import rankings, rosters, and more.
description: This week's 19 bug fixes and polish improvements touched the following areas of the site:

Calendar — Doubleheaders were being pushed too early in the season. The maths that splits them between the start and the end subtracted the fixed Week 1 game before halving, which quietly shrank the late half — four past seasons ended up with doubleheaders stacked in Weeks 1 to 3 while bye-free weeks at the end of the season went unused. The schedule builder could not cope with a season of a different length or a different division structure — it assumed 14 weeks and today’s divisions and gave up outright on anything else. Replaying the last fifteen years of NFL bye calendars found ten seasons it could not schedule at all. It now works the shape out from the format instead of assuming it. Schedule Release Day can no longer publish a schedule that missed a goal it could have hit. The lock previously checked only for structural breakage, so a season could leave a bye-free finale unused or decide a division race in September and still go live. Goals that were genuinely unachievable that year are still reported and still publish. The Schedule Builder now says plainly that it is a preview. It runs a shortened search so the page loads in time, while the release job runs a far longer one and produces a different schedule — and the page had been offering a copy-to-clipboard button as though the two were the same.

Live Scoring — Live Scoring stopped sliding sideways in a week with no games. Open it before kickoff and the empty "Scores will appear here when games begin" card ran wider than the phone, so the page scrolled horizontally with nothing to scroll to — the card's right edge parked just off screen, and a stray gray-and-blue bar sat along its top looking for all the world like a scrollbar. That bar is the win-probability split every real matchup card wears; with no matchup behind it there was nothing for it to show, so it's gone from the empty state, and the card now measures itself the same way the scoring cards do and fits the screen. The board behind it also stopped overflowing by a hair on the narrowest phones. Open a matchup on your phone and the little "Tracking · updated 37s ago" line — the one that proves the scores are still coming in — sat a full step to the left of the "All matchups" link right above it, hanging off the edge of the card like it had fallen out of the header. The header is one row that wraps on a narrow screen, and the indent had been attached to the back button instead of the row, so the moment the status dropped to its own line it lost the indent with it. The row carries it now, so both lines start at the same place — and on a wide screen the back link finally lines up with the team names below it too. A couple dozen players — D'Andre Swift, Tony Pollard, Cameron Dicker and three other kickers among them — were missing the id that links them to ESPN, so they quietly showed no box-score line on Live Scoring and went uncredited on their own touchdowns. All of them resolve now, and a test keeps it that way. On a phone, the two sides of a Live Scoring matchup never quite agreed on where a player's points sat — a name that wrapped onto a second line pushed its score down a hair, a name that didn't left it where it was, and the two columns read as slightly out of step all the way down. Worse on a narrow phone, where a name like Mike Washington Jr. needs three lines and drops that score a full line below his opponent's. Both sides of a matchup now share their rows outright, so a longer name, a wrapping box-score line, or a red-zone flag grows the row for both players at once and the numbers stay level. The box-score detail also moved below the score line rather than above it, which is where you'd look for it. Open the Bench on a Live Scoring matchup and the only thing telling you whose bench you were reading — the team name over each column — was the smallest text on the screen, a muted little label losing a shouting match with sixteen player names set larger than it was. The crest beside it was 16 pixels, roughly the size of the helmet logos tucked next to each player's game time. Both now read as a header: the team name in the display face at the same size as the players underneath it, over a 32-pixel crest you can identify at arm's length. Same two columns, same order, but you can tell at a glance which one is yours.

Import Rankings — The My Rank panel — the one where you set how much each ranking source counts — was taller than a phone screen, and it was anchored to the bottom, so everything it couldn't fit got pushed off the TOP. The title went first, then the X. An owner with nine sources loaded opened it, found the rows running past the edge with no way to scroll them back, and couldn't close the thing either. It now measures itself against the part of the screen you can actually see rather than the taller one your browser reports when its address bar is hidden, so the header and the Done button stay put and the list of sources scrolls between them. The Actions column on Import Rankings had drifted out of line with its own header, and the Average Rank row trailed a stray horizontal rule off to one side. Both are back in the grid where they belong.

Rosters — Player news in the player pop-up had no expiration date. Open a quiet backup and ESPN would happily hand back three stories from a season and a half ago — a training-camp battle he lost in 2024, presented with the same confidence as this morning's injury report. News now ages out: one month during the season, when a three-week-old note is already two depth charts behind, and three months in the offseason, when a June signing really is the freshest true thing about a player. And when there's genuinely nothing to show, the section stops holding open a tall empty box under the heading — it collapses to a single line telling you nothing turned up in the last 30 (or 90) days, so you know the search happened and came back empty instead of wondering whether it ran at all. Washington players had been quietly missing from their own games on Set Lineup. Every other roster spot told you who its player was up against that week; a Commanders player told you nothing — no opponent, no defensive matchup ranking — as if the week had forgotten him. Two halves of the app had been spelling the team differently, WAS on one side and WSH on the other, and a lookup that has to match exactly never did. They speak the same way now, and Washington's players get their week back like everybody else. Every row on Set Lineup tells you the game that player is walking into, and every one of them had the opponent's helmet parked out front with the words trailing behind it in a gray faint enough to read like a disclaimer — you had to lean in to tell a home game from a road game. The crest now sits inside the phrase, right after the vs or the @ where the team's name belongs, and the whole thing is in full-strength text like the rest of the row. Your starters and your bench also spell the opponent out now instead of leaving you to identify a 16-pixel logo on your phone: "vs LAC" beats a squint. Starters, bench, and the list of eligible replacements all read the same way, which they did not before. Set Lineup had two ways of losing your lineup on a future week, and an owner caught both in the same sitting: week 12 came up with nine empty slots and week 14 came up with nine players named 'Player 13592'. The names were the easy half — every page view re-asked MFL for the whole player file, and when that call got throttled the page had nothing left to print but the ID, even though the same names are sitting in a feed on our own disk. The empty week was the same throttling hitting the roster call instead. But the real find was underneath: the page asked MFL for your saved lineup with a request MFL has never accepted — myStarters is an import, not an export — and the error was swallowed, so it silently fell back to filling the slots with whoever projects best. That means it has never once shown you a lineup you submitted. It does now, for any week, and when there's genuinely nothing on file for that week it says so instead of dressing up a projection as your lineup. The franchise crest on a player modal's header was sitting directly behind the headshot, which left you looking at its edges. It is now about twice the size and offset to the left, so it tucks behind the player with most of the logo showing.

Rankings — The ranking columns on Free Agents finally look like they belong to the same table as everything else. Their headers are built on the fly once your board loads, and they had been missing the styling every other header gets — so "My Rank" and "FBG ®" came in oversized, mixed-case, and folded onto two lines on a phone while AGE, EXP and DRAFT sat neatly on one. They now read small, uppercase and gray like their neighbors, right-aligned over their numbers, and each title stays on a single line no matter how narrow the screen gets. Same fix in TheLeague and the AFL.

Other — The Computer Jocks finally have a real night look. Their crest was surviving dark mode on a generated green outline — a ring the site draws around any logo too dark to read on a dark card, which keeps a logo findable but is a floor, not a design. Somebody sat down and drew the thing properly instead: the lifter and the CPU wordmark redrawn to glow on black, ring baked into the artwork. It's the same file in both leagues, so the defending champs look identical whether you're reading TheLeague or the AFL, and the borrowed outline is gone from both. The GroupMe avatar got the matching cut while we were in there.

Design System & Theming — Hover a day on the Owner Activity chart in dark mode and the readout came up white text on a near-white box — legible only if you already knew what it said. The chart's tooltip was pinned to the darkest gray in the palette, and that palette flips in dark mode, so the "almost black" it asked for resolved to almost white while the text stayed white. It's now the same raised card surface the rest of the site uses, which fixes a quieter problem in light mode at the same time: the team dots in that readout are tuned to stand out against a card, so on the old dark chip the darker-jerseyed teams were dots you couldn't see.

The GroupMe avatar got the matching cut while we were in there.

Schefter Report — Schefter dropped a Pecking Order on the AFL in the middle of August, ranking a season that ended in December. The column runs every Tuesday year-round and it knew to sit out the offseason — it just had no idea it was the offseason. Its season clock rolls at Labor Day, so from February until then it still answers '2025', and the last completed week of 2025 is, unhelpfully, always available. The only thing that had kept it quiet all summer was that every past week already had a column on file; the first gap in the archive is what let it write one and buzz everybody's phone. It now checks that the season it's about to rank is actually being played, so the earliest column of any year is the Tuesday after Week 1, and the stray August issue has been pulled.

The chart's tooltip was pinned to the darkest gray in the palette, and that palette flips in dark mode, so the "almost black" it asked for resolved to almost white while the text stayed white. It's now the same raised card surface the rest of the site uses, which fixes a quieter problem in light mode at the same time: the team dots in that readout are tuned to stand out against a card, so on the old dark chip the darker-jerseyed teams were dots you couldn't see.

title: Weekly Fixes & Polish (Aug 18-24)
summary: 27 bug fixes and style improvements across navigation & routing, calendar, franchise pages, live scoring, and more.
description: This week's 27 bug fixes and polish improvements touched the following areas of the site:

Navigation & Routing — An owner spotted the AFL sneaking onto The League's Stats & Reports page. The League History shelf was carrying two cards that belong to the other league — Record Book and AFL Owners — and clicking either one went nowhere, because the link was built by gluing The League's address onto an AFL one. The shelf now lists only The League's own history pages: Franchises, Rivalries and Owners.

Calendar — Doubleheaders were being pushed too early in the season. The maths that splits them between the start and the end subtracted the fixed Week 1 game before halving, which quietly shrank the late half — four past seasons ended up with doubleheaders stacked in Weeks 1 to 3 while bye-free weeks at the end of the season went unused. The schedule builder could not cope with a season of a different length or a different division structure — it assumed 14 weeks and today’s divisions and gave up outright on anything else. Replaying the last fifteen years of NFL bye calendars found ten seasons it could not schedule at all. It now works the shape out from the format instead of assuming it. Schedule Release Day can no longer publish a schedule that missed a goal it could have hit. The lock previously checked only for structural breakage, so a season could leave a bye-free finale unused or decide a division race in September and still go live. Goals that were genuinely unachievable that year are still reported and still publish. The Schedule Builder now says plainly that it is a preview. It runs a shortened search so the page loads in time, while the release job runs a far longer one and produces a different schedule — and the page had been offering a copy-to-clipboard button as though the two were the same. The league calendar had the 2027 NFL Draft on April 22 — a Thursday, the fourth Thursday in April, very nearly the right answer and not the right answer. It's April 29. That matters more than a stray date on a calendar usually would, because our Rookie Draft isn't stored anywhere: it's computed off the NFL's opening night, nine days later, every year. So a draft that was a week early quietly made our draft a week early too — May 1 where it should read May 8 — in What's Next, on the calendar, and in anything Roger would have gotten around to reminding you about. The tell is that April was never the anchor. The NFL Draft tracks the Super Bowl, landing exactly 74 days after it every year since 2022, and the Super Bowl is the second Sunday in February. February 2027 opens on a Monday, which shoves that Sunday out to the 14th — the latest it can ever fall — and drags the draft to the fifth Thursday of April instead of the fourth. Run that against every year from 2022 to 2035 and the shortcut is wrong exactly once, in 2027, which is precisely why it sat there. Both years are now taken from ESPN instead of guessed, the Rookie Draft moves back to Saturday, May 8, and the nightly job that was supposed to catch this sort of thing has been fixed too: it had been failing every night for unrelated reasons, which is a fine way to make sure nobody looks at it the night it's finally right.

Franchise Pages — Midwestside's franchise history had been handing Nate a season he never played. His page opened on 2010 — a 2-16 Witch City Warlocks year that belonged to the owner before him — because the record of when he took over franchise 0010 started a year early. He arrived in 2011, the year the Warlocks became the Midwestside Connection, and 2011 is where his history starts now. The 2-16 goes back to the former owner where it belongs, and his career record loses it too: 95-117 instead of 97-133, with the 2010 Jerry Jones Award off his shelf. The other thing he noticed while he was down there: his first five seasons were wearing the Warlocks' pentagram. The art for that era was a copy of the logo it replaced, so 2011 through 2015 sat under an occult crest that was never his. Those years now wear the gold-ringed Midwestside photo — the same one the team wore right through 2024, because the banner Nate hung in 2011 is the banner still hanging today.

Live Scoring — Live Scoring stopped sliding sideways in a week with no games. Open it before kickoff and the empty "Scores will appear here when games begin" card ran wider than the phone, so the page scrolled horizontally with nothing to scroll to — the card's right edge parked just off screen, and a stray gray-and-blue bar sat along its top looking for all the world like a scrollbar. That bar is the win-probability split every real matchup card wears; with no matchup behind it there was nothing for it to show, so it's gone from the empty state, and the card now measures itself the same way the scoring cards do and fits the screen. The board behind it also stopped overflowing by a hair on the narrowest phones. Open a matchup on your phone and the little "Tracking · updated 37s ago" line — the one that proves the scores are still coming in — sat a full step to the left of the "All matchups" link right above it, hanging off the edge of the card like it had fallen out of the header. The header is one row that wraps on a narrow screen, and the indent had been attached to the back button instead of the row, so the moment the status dropped to its own line it lost the indent with it. The row carries it now, so both lines start at the same place — and on a wide screen the back link finally lines up with the team names below it too. A couple dozen players — D'Andre Swift, Tony Pollard, Cameron Dicker and three other kickers among them — were missing the id that links them to ESPN, so they quietly showed no box-score line on Live Scoring and went uncredited on their own touchdowns. All of them resolve now, and a test keeps it that way. On a phone, the two sides of a Live Scoring matchup never quite agreed on where a player's points sat — a name that wrapped onto a second line pushed its score down a hair, a name that didn't left it where it was, and the two columns read as slightly out of step all the way down. Worse on a narrow phone, where a name like Mike Washington Jr. needs three lines and drops that score a full line below his opponent's. Both sides of a matchup now share their rows outright, so a longer name, a wrapping box-score line, or a red-zone flag grows the row for both players at once and the numbers stay level. The box-score detail also moved below the score line rather than above it, which is where you'd look for it. Open the Bench on a Live Scoring matchup and the only thing telling you whose bench you were reading — the team name over each column — was the smallest text on the screen, a muted little label losing a shouting match with sixteen player names set larger than it was. The crest beside it was 16 pixels, roughly the size of the helmet logos tucked next to each player's game time. Both now read as a header: the team name in the display face at the same size as the players underneath it, over a 32-pixel crest you can identify at arm's length. Same two columns, same order, but you can tell at a glance which one is yours.

Import Rankings — The My Rank panel — the one where you set how much each ranking source counts — was taller than a phone screen, and it was anchored to the bottom, so everything it couldn't fit got pushed off the TOP. The title went first, then the X. An owner with nine sources loaded opened it, found the rows running past the edge with no way to scroll them back, and couldn't close the thing either. It now measures itself against the part of the screen you can actually see rather than the taller one your browser reports when its address bar is hidden, so the header and the Done button stay put and the list of sources scrolls between them. The Actions column on Import Rankings had drifted out of line with its own header, and the Average Rank row trailed a stray horizontal rule off to one side. Both are back in the grid where they belong.

Rosters — Player news in the player pop-up had no expiration date. Open a quiet backup and ESPN would happily hand back three stories from a season and a half ago — a training-camp battle he lost in 2024, presented with the same confidence as this morning's injury report. News now ages out: one month during the season, when a three-week-old note is already two depth charts behind, and three months in the offseason, when a June signing really is the freshest true thing about a player. And when there's genuinely nothing to show, the section stops holding open a tall empty box under the heading — it collapses to a single line telling you nothing turned up in the last 30 (or 90) days, so you know the search happened and came back empty instead of wondering whether it ran at all. Washington players had been quietly missing from their own games on Set Lineup. Every other roster spot told you who its player was up against that week; a Commanders player told you nothing — no opponent, no defensive matchup ranking — as if the week had forgotten him. Two halves of the app had been spelling the team differently, WAS on one side and WSH on the other, and a lookup that has to match exactly never did. They speak the same way now, and Washington's players get their week back like everybody else. Every row on Set Lineup tells you the game that player is walking into, and every one of them had the opponent's helmet parked out front with the words trailing behind it in a gray faint enough to read like a disclaimer — you had to lean in to tell a home game from a road game. The crest now sits inside the phrase, right after the vs or the @ where the team's name belongs, and the whole thing is in full-strength text like the rest of the row. Your starters and your bench also spell the opponent out now instead of leaving you to identify a 16-pixel logo on your phone: "vs LAC" beats a squint. Starters, bench, and the list of eligible replacements all read the same way, which they did not before. Throwback Week wasn't throwing all the way back on the Set Lineup screen. Week 4 correctly gave both teams their old names and their old colors, then painted the modern logo behind the players anyway — so the Pigskins, whose throwback name is just 'Pacific Pigskins' again, showed no sign of throwing back at all. The crest was the one piece of the old identity nobody had wired up: the overlay swapped the team's icon, but that banner reads a different field, and that field kept pointing at today's mark. It now wears the era's own logo, and each team's 2013-or-whenever crest sits behind its player like it was supposed to. The matchup banner on Set Lineup was showing you the same two faces every week, and both of them were quarterbacks. It picked whoever projected highest, and since a starting QB projects ten points clear of anyone else on a roster, the tight end who is the best tight end in football never once got the panel. It now casts by rank within position, weighed against how many the league actually has to start — we start one quarterback and four backs and receivers, so QB12 is a guy you'd bench where WR12 is a stud, and the panel finally knows the difference. The line under the name says which — WR1 · CIN · 18.0 PROJ — so you can see why that face is up there. Thirteen of sixteen teams get a new headliner out of it, and a genuinely elite quarterback still gets his panel. The two headshots also moved out to the far edges of the banner instead of standing in the middle of it, which finally lets your franchise crest read behind them instead of being a rumor. Set Lineup had two ways of losing your lineup on a future week, and an owner caught both in the same sitting: week 12 came up with nine empty slots and week 14 came up with nine players named 'Player 13592'. The names were the easy half — every page view re-asked MFL for the whole player file, and when that call got throttled the page had nothing left to print but the ID, even though the same names are sitting in a feed on our own disk. The empty week was the same throttling hitting the roster call instead. But the real find was underneath: the page asked MFL for your saved lineup with a request MFL has never accepted — myStarters is an import, not an export — and the error was swallowed, so it silently fell back to filling the slots with whoever projects best. That means it has never once shown you a lineup you submitted. It does now, for any week, and when there's genuinely nothing on file for that week it says so instead of dressing up a projection as your lineup. At one specific browser width — right at the tablet breakpoint — the GM/Coach switch on the roster page was sliced in half by the top edge of the card it sits in. It stays inside the card at every width now. The franchise crest on a player modal's header was sitting directly behind the headshot, which left you looking at its edges. It is now about twice the size and offset to the left, so it tucks behind the player with most of the logo showing. Every team's player-modal header now takes its colour from the team's actual brand rather than from the colour used on charts, which is picked to stand out on a graph and isn't always a colour the team wears — Vitside were opening in a pink that appears nowhere in their kit. Most bands shift, and three lead with a deliberate choice: Midwestside black with gold trim, Vitside black with red, the Gridiron Geeks blue with orange. The crest sits a little smaller too.

Rankings — Projected Free Agents was ignoring your rankings board. The report had its own private idea of which ranking columns to draw — the first eight it could find — so it showed an Average column nobody asked for and every source you had deliberately unticked in the My Rank editor, eight columns of it running off the right edge of the screen. Free Agents has honored your board for months; this page never got the message. It now uses the same rule: My Rank plus the sources actually feeding it, nothing you turned off, and the table fits on the screen again. On a phone the ranking headers hide along with their numbers instead of hanging around over the wrong columns. The ranking columns on Free Agents finally look like they belong to the same table as everything else. Their headers are built on the fly once your board loads, and they had been missing the styling every other header gets — so "My Rank" and "FBG ®" came in oversized, mixed-case, and folded onto two lines on a phone while AGE, EXP and DRAFT sat neatly on one. They now read small, uppercase and gray like their neighbors, right-aligned over their numbers, and each title stays on a single line no matter how narrow the screen gets. Same fix in TheLeague and the AFL.

Other — The Computer Jocks finally have a real night look. Their crest was surviving dark mode on a generated green outline — a ring the site draws around any logo too dark to read on a dark card, which keeps a logo findable but is a floor, not a design. Somebody sat down and drew the thing properly instead: the lifter and the CPU wordmark redrawn to glow on black, ring baked into the artwork. It's the same file in both leagues, so the defending champs look identical whether you're reading TheLeague or the AFL, and the borrowed outline is gone from both. The GroupMe avatar got the matching cut while we were in there.

Design System & Theming — Hover a day on the Owner Activity chart in dark mode and the readout came up white text on a near-white box — legible only if you already knew what it said. The chart's tooltip was pinned to the darkest gray in the palette, and that palette flips in dark mode, so the "almost black" it asked for resolved to almost white while the text stayed white. It's now the same raised card surface the rest of the site uses, which fixes a quieter problem in light mode at the same time: the team dots in that readout are tuned to stand out against a card, so on the old dark chip the darker-jerseyed teams were dots you couldn't see.

title: The Schedule Builder Learned What It Was Getting Wrong
summary: A rebuild let the scheduler place each rivalry game in a week that suits those two rosters instead of forcing everyone into the same weeks. Then it produced a season with zero division games on bye weeks and a division race that ended in Week 4 — so a new rule went in, and the schedule you already have turns out to have been right.
description: A hidden assumption ran through every schedule this league has ever generated: division games came in complete rounds, so if your rivalry game was in Week 9, so was everyone else’s. Nobody chose that. It fell out of how the builder assembled a season.

The rebuilt version does not need that. A week only has to give every franchise exactly one game — not the same KIND of game — so a week can hold two rivalry games and four ordinary ones, and each matchup can go where those two rosters are healthy.

Turned loose, it found something uncomfortable. It produced a season with ZERO division games on bye weeks and not a single starter missing from a rivalry game. It did that by cramming all 48 division games into Weeks 1 through 4 and Week 12, leaving Weeks 5 to 11, 13 and 14 without one, and the finale with none at all. Perfect on paper. A division race decided in September.

The old builder had prevented that for free, by construction, which is exactly why nobody had ever written it down as a rule. So it is written down now: every franchise plays roughly half its division games after the midpoint, ranked just below keeping them off bye weeks.

With that rule in place the arithmetic settles it. A 50/50 split needs 24 division games after Week 7, only one clean week remains that late, and it holds 16 — so at least eight must land on a bye week. Eight is exactly what the current schedule has. The schedule you are playing was already the right answer; we just proved it instead of assuming it.

title: The Scheduler Now Knows Who Is Actually Missing
summary: Next year’s schedule is built against your projected starting nine instead of your whole roster, and it actively hunts for weeks where neither side of a rivalry game is missing anyone. Replayed on 2026 it cuts missing starters in division games by nearly a third.
description: The old scheduler asked “does this week have NFL byes in it?” That question is nearly useless for a 24-man roster, because a 24-man roster almost always has somebody out. Measured on The League’s 2026 rosters, only 10% of team-week combinations were fully clean, and Weeks 8, 11 and 13 had none at all. Every week looked equally bad, so nothing could be optimised.

It now asks a better question: is either of THESE two teams missing a projected starter that week? Counting the starting nine instead of the whole roster takes The League from 10% usable weeks to 41%, and it unlocks Weeks 8, 11 and 13 entirely.

The AFL is unaffected, and that is the correct answer rather than an oversight. The AFL reveals its schedule before its draft, so a roster is seven keepers — fewer players than there are starting slots, which means everyone kept is a starter. Whole-roster and starter counts agree exactly there.

On top of that the optimiser now scores rivalry games specifically: starters missing from a division game, both sides added together. The old fairness measure could not see this at all, because it only checked whether the two teams were EQUALLY hurt — two rivals both missing three starters scored perfectly, which is exactly the game nobody wants to play. Replayed on 2026 the AFL goes from 58 missing starters across its division games to 40, and from 94 to 99 rivalry games with both rosters whole.

The 2026 schedules are untouched — locked, pasted and being played. This applies to the next one. Still to come: letting different teams play their division games in different weeks, which is a deeper rebuild of how rounds are constructed.

title: Schefter Learned to Point at Things
summary: Every Schefter column now links to the page it's about, and works in the tool that answers whatever question the paragraph just raised. His schedule release article somehow never linked to the schedule release page. That's fixed, and so is the reason it happened.
description: Claude Schefter filed eight paragraphs about the 2026 schedule — the four games to circle, the rivalry records, the bye-week math — and never once told you where to go read the thing. The schedule release page was right there. The column existed to announce it. Not a link in sight.

It turned out not to be a slip in one article. Searching the entire published feed for a link — 396 posts, every column he has ever filed, both leagues — turned up exactly zero. He had never linked to anything. He would name a roster crunch and not point at the rosters, call out dead weight and not point at the dead money report, and finish a cut-watch column three days from a deadline without once mentioning the calendar.

Now every article type declares where it points before a word is written. The page the column is about gets linked near the top and again at the end, and the pages it touches on the way through get linked where they come up. Go back and read the 2026 schedule release now: the opening line is the link, Throwback Week goes to your throwback settings, the rivalry section goes to the rivalry pages, and the closer hands you the full week-by-week grid. The three cut-watch columns from August got the same treatment — over-the-limit rosters, dead weight, a bloated receiver room that the trade builder has opinions about.

The second half of the job is new: Schefter is now expected to plug the site. Not with a paragraph of housekeeping bolted to the end — with the tool that answers the question he just raised. Grading your auction and pointing at the salary benchmarks. Naming the guy you're about to lose and pointing at the free agent board. He picks the ones that fit the story and skips the rest, because a plug he had to wedge in reads like an ad, and nobody clicks a columnist who sounds like an ad.

Links he makes up don't survive. He writes from a list of real pages, and anything that isn't on it gets quietly unwrapped before publishing — the sentence still reads, it just stops promising a page that doesn't exist. And if he forgets the main link entirely, the way he did in August, it gets put back in for him. A Schefter column with nothing to click is no longer something that can happen.
imageAlt: The 2026 schedule release article on The Schefter Report, headlined “The 2026 Schedule Is Here. Four Games Will Define It.” under Claude Schefter’s byline. Three phrases in the prose are blue underlined links: “The 2026 schedule for The League is official” in the opening line, “Throwback Week” inside the Week 4 paragraph about Bring the Pain at Vitside Mafia, and “The rivalry renewals are stacked this season” opening the rivalry section.

title: The Schedule Now Shows Its Work
summary: Schedule Release Day used to tell you how many division games dodged the NFL byes and stop there. It now tells you how many did NOT, what percentage that is, and how many of those the format left no way to avoid — plus the ten rules the draw had to satisfy, in the order they beat each other.
description: The old line on the schedule release page read '84 of 84 possible division games clear of NFL byes' and it was true, which is exactly the problem. Read it quickly and it sounds like a clean sweep. It is not: 36 of the AFL’s 120 division games are played on weeks with NFL byes, and the page never said so.

Both numbers are now on the board, with the part that actually matters underneath: all 36 are FORCED. A franchise has eight bye-free game slots, the constitution spends one of them on the Week 1 cross-conference game, and it plays ten division games. The math runs out before the calendar does. Every legal way of drawing the season lands on the same 36 — we checked all 336 of them — so this is the floor, not a miss.

The League’s eight are the opposite: nothing forces them. They are the price of ending the season on rivalry games in a year when Weeks 13 and 14 both carry byes. You cannot have the all-division finish and a perfectly clean sheet, and the league picked the finish. The page now says which kind of number you are looking at instead of leaving you to guess.

Underneath sits the whole rulebook, ranked: the format at the top, then the hard rules that get a schedule rejected outright, then the things the optimiser maximises, then the preferences, then home-and-away, which is settled exactly once everything above it is fixed. Ten rules, five tiers. Nearly every 'why is my schedule like this' question turns out to be a higher rule beating a lower one, and now you can see which.
imageAlt: The AFL Schedule Release page. A row of fact tiles reads 204 games, doubleheaders in weeks 1, 2 and 12, 84 of 84 possible division games clear of NFL byes, and a new tile reading 36 of 120 (30%) division games on an NFL bye with the caption 'all 36 forced by the format — the floor, not a miss', then home games 8 to 9. Below it a section headed 'The rules this draw had to satisfy' lists ten numbered cards in priority order, each with a coloured left stripe and a tier label: two THE FORMAT rules, three HARD RULE, three MAXIMISED, one PREFERENCE and one SETTLED EXACTLY.

title: Your Crest, Not Cleveland's
summary: Open a player from your roster and the modal header now wears the franchise that owns him — your colors in the gradient, your crest behind the headshot, instead of a wall of his NFL team's paint. The contract sheet picks up the same header, and on Throwback Week the whole thing goes vintage.
description: The banner across the top of a player modal has always been a nice piece of work — team gradient, ghost wordmark, headshot cut out and floating. It just kept telling you something you already knew. You clicked a name on YOUR roster page, under YOUR crest, on a row that already carries the little NFL logo, and the header answered with a wall of Ravens purple. Sixteen owners, one league, and every modal looked like the NFL app.

Now the band belongs to the fantasy team. The gradient runs off the franchise's own color and the crest sits behind the cutout as a watermark, so a Pigskins player opens in Pigskins red under the pigskin, and a Midwestside player opens in gold under the MWS ring. The pro team hasn't gone anywhere — the helmet logo and the city are still on the line under the name, and the ghost wordmark behind it all still reads QB RAVENS. Click into a free agent and nothing changes at all: nobody owns him, so he keeps the NFL colors he's earned.

Two things here are The League only, because they are The League's furniture. The first is the contract sheet. Tapping the action button on a roster row used to open a plain white card with a small round headshot chip — a different-looking modal for the same player you were just looking at. It now opens with the exact same band, and it stays put at the top while the flow scrolls underneath. The three stat tiles — salary, years, designation — come with it, which matters more than it sounds: the old version hid them on the very step where you pick between Veteran Extension, Move to IR, Cut Player and Trade Player. You were being asked to choose without the three numbers the choice turns on. AFL owners have no contracts to declare, so there is no sheet there to match — the AFL's own action menu keeps the look it has.

The second is Throwback Week, which only The League runs. On that week the crest and the colors swap to whatever era your team is wearing — the one you picked in Throwback Settings, or the default the commissioner seeded — the same as the scoreboard and the lineup faceoffs. Open a player on Week 4 and he's under the 2013 mark in the 2013 red, and nobody had to remember to flip a switch.

One bit of housekeeping under the hood, and it applies in both leagues. A handful of franchise colors are far too bright to put white type on — Midwestside's gold sits at 1.5:1 — so the gradient anchor gets darkened just far enough to clear the readability floor. And where a team's primary is a flat grey or black, which several are in both leagues, the band reaches for their secondary instead; otherwise three different AFL teams opened to the same near-black header.
imageAlt: The contract action modal for Lamar Jackson on the roster page. The header band is a deep-ink-to-red gradient in the Pacific Pigskins' colors with the Pigskins crest watermarked behind his cutout headshot, his name and age pill in white, the Ravens helmet logo beside “Baltimore · QB”, and “Louisville” below. Under the band sit a Step 1 of ? indicator and three stat tiles reading $5.00M salary, 3 years and Standard designation, then a Contract Action list with Veteran Extension, Move to IR and Cut Player.

title: The Schedule Is Graded Now, Not Just Explained
summary: The scheduling rules are goals now — ranked, and scored against the season they actually produced. Every release page shows how that year did on each one, because the NFL moves the bye calendar and the same goal is easy one year and impossible the next. Plus a new goal for 2027.
description: A list of rules with no outcomes is a list of promises, and this one kept looking like a schedule breaking them. It is not. The league does not control the NFL’s bye calendar, so the same goal is trivial one year and unreachable the next — and a page that never says which is which reads as an accusation.

So they are goals, they are ranked, and every season is graded on the schedule release page against the ones that were in force when it was drawn. Each goal now carries a verdict: MET, AS FAR AS THE CALENDAR ALLOWED, NOT ACHIEVABLE THIS YEAR, or OPTIMISED for the soft ones where inventing a pass mark would be less honest than showing the number. The AFL’s 2026 schedule scores eight met and two optimised. The League’s scores six met, two partial, two optimised — and the two partials are things the calendar decided, not things anyone got wrong.

Top of the list, and it is not close: no doubleheader lands on an NFL bye week. A doubleheader pays the bye penalty twice. In a year when no league-wide week works, the commissioner has staggered doubleheaders franchise by franchise so each team plays its two games in a week its own roster is whole — a last resort, built by hand, and still better than the alternative. Next is getting division games off bye weeks, which the AFL cannot fully do and The League can only do by giving up its all-division finish.

New for 2027, and written into the constitution already: the division games that cannot dodge a bye week take the LIGHTEST bye weeks — ideally ones with only two NFL teams out instead of six. Replayed over the last five seasons it improves three of them, 2024 by more than half.

The 2026 schedules are not re-drawn — they are locked and being played. They are graded against the ten goals that existed when they were made, and the new one is listed separately as adopted afterwards. Every goal is the same in both leagues; only the outcomes differ.
imageAlt: The AFL Schedule Release page. Under the heading 'The goals, ranked — and how 2026 did', ten numbered cards each show a goal, a coloured tier stripe and label, and a verdict chip. Examples: 'No doubleheader falls on an NFL bye week' with MET — Weeks 1, 2, 12, none with an NFL bye; 'Division games take every bye-free slot the format leaves them' with MET — 36 of 120 division games (30%) fall on a bye week, every one forced by the format. Two goals are marked OPTIMISED rather than met or missed. A dashed box at the bottom reads 'Adopted since this schedule was drawn' and lists the lightest-bye-week goal as applying from 2027.

title: Schedule Release Day Is a Real Day Now
summary: Both leagues get an annual Schedule Release Day — a countdown page that hits zero, locks one schedule for everybody, and puts four games on the board worth circling, rivalry records and all. Same draw for every owner, no reshuffles.
description: The NFL turns its schedule release into a two-hour prime-time special. We used to do ours by way of a commissioner quietly saving a form in May and somebody noticing in August. That is over. Both leagues now have a Schedule Release Day on the calendar, with a page that counts down to it — find it under Offseason War Room in the menu. The League goes June 1; the AFL goes the Sunday two weeks before the National League draft, a date that moves with Labor Day every year, same as the draft it is pinned to.

Open the page before the day and there is a clock — days, hours, minutes, seconds. When it hits zero the schedule locks, and locked is the whole point. The draw is built by an optimizer that could produce a hundred different valid seasons, so if everyone hit a button and got their own, fifteen of sixteen owners would be studying a year that never happens. One schedule gets locked, everybody sees that one, and the copy-and-paste block the commissioner sends to MFL is the exact same one on your screen.

The first thing you get is the tease: four games, four different weeks, each one wearing both franchises’ colors and crests and a line saying why it is there. And the why is not just this year’s records — it is the whole history. The League’s 2026 board opens on a division game in a Week 1 doubleheader, runs the championship rematch in Week 9, and closes in Week 14 with a division title on the line. Records come straight off the same rivalry math the Rivalries pages use, and where the archives disagree with themselves about a pairing — which happens for eighteen of them, a leftover from a franchise identity that changed slots years ago — the card simply says nothing rather than pick a number.

Week 4 gets its own reserved slot, because Week 4 is Throwback Week. The card shows that game the way it will actually be played — old logos, old names, old colors — and the schedule picks it by rivalry rather than by record, so it is the oldest, closest series in the week rather than whoever happens to be good. In 2026 that is Bring the Pain at a Vitside Mafia playing as BOYZ II MEN: fifteen meetings, separated by exactly one game.

Under the tease, the receipts. The schedule is not a shuffle — it is optimized against the constitution and against the NFL’s bye calendar, and the page shows how it did. The League’s 2026 season: 144 games, doubleheaders in Weeks 1, 2, 3 and 12, 40 of a possible 48 division games played on weeks with no NFL byes, and every team with nine home games and nine road games. No more losing a division game because four of your starters were on vacation that Sunday.

Then the full week-by-week grid, so you can find your own season without waiting for MFL to catch up. Any signed-in owner can see all of it. The paste block is commissioner-only, for the obvious reason that saving it in MFL overwrites the entire schedule and there is no undo. And when the paste does land, Claude Schefter files the release column — four games, the rivalries the draw renews, and the records to go with them — and drops it in the chat.

title: Both Halves of a Double-Header, Finally
summary: On a week where you play twice, Set Lineup now shows both games instead of one — and both leagues' lineup pages carry the matchup panel. Swipe between games on your phone, click the arrows on a laptop, and watch your projected total move on every card at once.
description: Double-headers are two opponents, two results, one lineup. TheLeague runs them in Weeks 1 through 3 and Week 13; the AFL has three of its own. Set Lineup never let on. It found the first game with your name on it, drew the matchup panel, and stopped — so half the week you were setting a lineup for simply wasn't on the page. If your second opponent was the one you needed to worry about, the page had nothing to say about them.

Now there's a card for each game. On a phone they sit side by side and snap under your thumb, with a dot for each and a small “Game 1 of 2” that keeps up as you swipe. On anything with a mouse, arrows sit on the panel and click through the same cards. A normal single-game week looks exactly as it always has — no dots, no arrows, nothing new to learn.

Each card knows its own game. Home and away follow the schedule, so you're on the right side of each scoreboard, and the projected total facing you is that opponent's, not a number borrowed from the other game. The one number both cards share is yours: MFL takes one lineup for the week and scores it twice, so every swap you make ticks your total on both cards at once. Watching one go up while the other sat there stale would have been its own kind of lie.

AFL owners get the whole thing at once. That page had no matchup panel at all — you set nine slots with no idea who they were pointed at. Now the same strip sits above the slots, each side wearing its franchise's colors and crest, with the projected score under it and a player of the game from each roster. Two opponents means two of those faceoffs, which is what a double-header week actually looks like.
